brief.title: A new US Congress changes the odds.
brief.text: Democrats won both houses in the November 3 midterms. Expect more AI oversight hearings and pushes on privacy and kids' safety, and less chance of Congress overriding state AI laws. Any bill still faces a veto and the Senate filibuster. The lame-duck KIDS Act faces fading Senate prospects.
sources: Bloomberg Law: KIDS Act lame duck

brief.title: UK cyber bill is one Commons vote from Royal Assent.
brief.text: The Commons was scheduled to consider 112 Lords amendments on November 24 — the last step before Royal Assent. The government moved to disagree with both Lords defeats. No date for Royal Assent yet, but the bill must pass by April 29, 2027 or lapse.

brief.title: Canada moves its online safety bill and funds a regulator.
brief.text: Bill C-34 is in committee with hearings underway (Nov 17, 19, 24). Bill C-36 second reading has begun in the House. Budget 2026 funds the commission that would enforce both. Canada also signed a voluntary AI-incident early-warning declaration on November 9.

brief.title: Colorado finalizes AI rules; White House SI deadline looms.
brief.text: Colorado's AG adopted 76 pages of AI rules on November 19; both statutes take effect January 1, 2027. The White House legislative-language deadline on defining "super intelligence" falls around November 28, and the Super Intelligence Force 120-day report is due in early February 2027.

CA: PIPEDA in force; C-36 at second reading (debate began Nov 2026); Children's Privacy Code issued Oct 2026; surveillance pricing guidance coming
No AI law; national strategy, transparency consultation closed Sept 23 (results pending), agentic AI resolution at GPA Nov 2026
C-34 Safe Social Media Act: committee hearings underway (Nov 17, 19, 24+)
Competition Act; Bureau studying algorithmic pricing; OPC also consulting on surveillance pricing
Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act passed June 2026; regulations pending
CUSMA on annual review; streaming payments being scrapped
US: No federal law; about 20 state laws in force

State laws (CO, CA, TX); CO AG rules adopted Nov 19 (take effect Jan 1, 2027); federal preemption less likely after Democratic midterm wins; voluntary safety accord; FTC and state AGs using consumer law
TAKE IT DOWN Act in force; KIDS Act passed House — Senate prospects fading in lame duck
Bloomberg Law: KIDS Act lame duck
Antitrust law enforced through courts; Google search remedies under appeal by both sides
CIRCIA final reporting rule still at White House review as of mid-November 2026; not yet published
Using tariffs against foreign tech rules and taxes
UK: UK GDPR amended by Data (Use and Access) Act, phasing in
No AI bill; sector regulators and sandboxes
Online Safety Act enforced (court upheld Ofcom data powers Oct 30); under-16 ban coming spring 2027
DMCC Act: first conduct requirements on Google; CMA Microsoft consultation closed Nov 13 — final designation decision due Feb 13, 2027
Cyber Security and Resilience Bill: Commons considers Lords amendments Nov 24 — last step before Royal Assent

watch.what: UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill: Commons voted on Lords amendments Nov 24
watch.why: If accepted, Royal Assent follows shortly. If the Commons disagrees with Lords amendments, ping-pong between chambers continues. The bill must pass by April 29, 2027.

watch.what: White House legislative language defining 'super intelligence'
watch.why: The 60-day deadline from the September 29 executive order falls around November 28. The definition will determine what technologies federal AI laws cover.

watch.what: Super Intelligence Force 120-day report on AI risks and opportunities
watch.why: First sign of whether US federal AI oversight goes beyond voluntary commitments.

watch.what: Colorado AG final AI and chatbot rules effective
watch.why: Rules adopted Nov 19, 2026. Both SB 26-189 (automated decision-making) and HB 26-1263 (Chatbot Safety Act) take effect Jan 1; first chatbot reports due July 1, 2027.

watch.what: CMA final SMS designation decision for Microsoft business software
watch.why: Consultation closed Nov 13. Designation would trigger powers to impose conduct requirements on Windows, Microsoft 365, Copilot, Teams and security software.

watch.what: 119th US Congress ends; lame-duck KIDS Act / KOSA window closes
watch.why: Senate prospects for the KIDS Act are fading. Unpassed bills die when the new Congress starts January 3.

watch.what: Comments close on Canada's Children's Privacy Code
watch.why: The OPC may revise the Code after comments.
Sets 72-hour incident and 24-hour ransom-payment reporting for critical infrastructure; still at White House OMB review as of mid-November.

watch.what: Canada Bill C-34 committee hearings; C-36 second reading
watch.why: C-34 (CHPC) hearings underway (Nov 17, 19, 24+); C-36 second reading debate begun. Committee hearings shape Canada's online safety and privacy rules.

watch.what: Canada's policy direction to the CRTC on streaming
watch.why: Replaces the scrapped streamer contribution rules.
First sign of the Democratic agenda on AI oversight, privacy and kids' online safety.

items.title: Democrats win both houses of Congress, raising the odds of tech oversight
items.what: Democrats won control of the House and Senate in the November 3 midterms. AP counts on November 9 gave them 254 House seats and 54 Senate seats, with some races still uncalled. AI and data centres were a notable campaign issue. The new Congress sits from January 2027.
items.why: Expect more hearings on AI companies and renewed pushes on federal privacy and children's online safety. Federal preemption of state AI laws becomes less likely. Any new law still needs the President's signature and, in most cases, 60 Senate votes, so state laws will keep doing most of the work.
expert: AP tally as of Nov. 9, 2026: House D 254, R 162 (19 uncalled); Senate D 54, R 44 (2 uncalled). Final margins may shift.

The White House's March 2026 legislative framework (preemption of burdensome state AI laws) will lack a friendly Congress; the DOJ AI Litigation Task Force route under the Dec. 2025 executive order is unaffected.
Pending bills (KIDS Act, Senate KOSA) die at the end of the current Congress unless passed in the lame-duck session. Senate prospects are fading as of late November 2026.
items.cite: 2026 US midterm elections, Nov. 3, 2026.

items.title: Colorado AG adopts final AI and chatbot rules, effective January 1, 2027
items.what: On November 19 Colorado's Attorney General adopted 76 pages of rules implementing two AI laws: SB 26-189 (automated decision-making in consequential decisions) and HB 26-1263 (Chatbot Safety Act). Both statutes take effect January 1, 2027. The rules take effect 20 days after the Secretary of State publishes them, once the AG files a formal opinion.
items.why: If you use automated tools to make consequential decisions about Colorado residents — in jobs, credit, housing or health care — you need notices, an appeal process and human review in place by January 1. If you offer a chatbot to users, check the chatbot disclosure and safeguards rules.
expert: SB 26-189: pre-use disclosure of automated decision-making technology, post-adverse-decision explanation, correction rights, human review on request; three-year record retention. Attorney General enforcement under CCPA; 60-day cure period until January 1, 2030.
HB 26-1263 (Chatbot Safety Act): disclosure and safeguards requirements for conversational AI services; first reports due July 1, 2027.
Rules include that ID-only age checks for chatbots are banned (alternative verification required).
Rules not yet formally published with the Secretary of State as of November 24, so the precise effective date is not confirmed. Treat January 1 as the planning target.
items.cite: Colorado AG, final rules under SB 26-189 and HB 26-1263 (adopted Nov. 19, 2026), 4 CCR 904-6.

items.title: UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill: Commons considers Lords amendments today
items.what: The Commons was scheduled to consider 112 Lords amendments on November 24 — the last parliamentary step before Royal Assent. The government moved to disagree with both Lords defeats (a regime-wide review amendment and a foreign powers register). If the Commons agrees on the text, Royal Assent follows shortly. If it disagrees with Lords amendments, the bill enters ping-pong. No date for Royal Assent is confirmed; the bill must pass by April 29, 2027 or lapse.
items.why: If the bill becomes law, managed IT service providers and key suppliers to UK essential services face new reporting duties and possible direct regulation. Watch for commencement regulations to set when obligations start.
expert: Commons debate capped at three hours on November 24. Government moved to disagree with two Lords amendments (regime-wide review; foreign powers register).
112 total Lords amendments: 5 from Grand Committee, 103 from Report Stage, 4 from Third Reading.

Amends the Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018. Extends scope to managed service providers and designated critical suppliers; tightens incident reporting (initial notice within 24 hours, full report within 72 hours).
Carry-over extension granted November 4, 2026, extending parliamentary deadline to April 29, 2027.
Outcome of November 24 vote not yet confirmed as of publication of this update.
items.cite: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill (DSIT).

items.title: CMA Microsoft consultation closed Nov 13; final designation decision due Feb 13, 2027
items.what: The CMA provisionally found that Microsoft has strategic market status in business software, from Windows and Office to Teams, Copilot, security and server products. The public consultation closed November 13. The CMA must issue its final designation decision by February 13, 2027.
items.why: Organizations that buy Microsoft products could gain more choice over AI assistants, security tools and cloud licensing. If designation is confirmed, the CMA will consult on conduct requirements before imposing them.
expert: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, Part 1. Investigation covered PC operating systems, productivity suites, security software, server operating systems and relational databases.

Indicative roadmap of possible interventions: security-product bundling, wider software bundling, interoperability for developers, fair competition with Copilot for rival AI providers, and cloud licensing terms.
Designation does not imply wrongdoing. Consultation closed 5pm, November 13, 2026; statutory deadline February 13, 2027.
The CMA will review responses before issuing its final decision; conduct requirements, if any, would follow a further process after designation.
items.cite: CMA, proposed SMS decision: Microsoft's business software ecosystem (Oct. 16, 2026). Consultation closed Nov. 13, 2026.

items.title: UK High Court backs Ofcom's power to demand data from Meta, X and TikTok
items.what: In the first court test of Ofcom's information powers under the Online Safety Act, the High Court rejected challenges by Meta, X and TikTok to notices demanding data on platform activity and content moderation.
items.why: Ofcom's information requests are hard to resist. If you run a regulated service in the UK, treat information notices as binding and plan for the cost of answering them.
expert: R (Meta, X and TikTok) v Ofcom, judgment handed down Oct. 30, 2026 (Singh LJ and Collins Rice J). Notices issued Feb. 10, 2026 under s. 100 OSA 2023.
The court accepted the notices engaged Article 8 ECHR but held the interference proportionate. The ruling covers these notices, not the Act as a whole.
Meta said it was disappointed; no appeal reported as of Nov. 24. A separate Meta challenge to how Ofcom calculates OSA fees is ongoing.
items.cite: R (Meta Platforms, X Corp and TikTok) v Ofcom [High Court, Oct. 30, 2026].

items.title: Canada's Budget 2026 funds a new digital safety regulator
items.what: The federal budget proposes $176.3 million over five years, plus $29.3 million a year ongoing, to set up the Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission and enforce Bill C-34. Under Bill C-36 the same body would also take over private-sector privacy enforcement. The budget also proposes a national anti-fraud strategy and tougher anti-fraud duties for telecoms.
items.why: Funding signals the government intends to pass C-34 and C-36, but neither is law and most budget measures still need legislation. Nothing changes for businesses yet.
expert: Budget 2026, Chapter 5: $176.3M over five years from 2026–27 and $29.3M ongoing, to Canadian Heritage, for the Commission's Safe Social Media Act work.
Anti-fraud measures bring banks, telecoms and digital platforms into a National Anti-Fraud Strategy; implementing details not yet published.
items.cite: Budget 2026, Chapter 5 (tabled Nov. 5, 2026).

items.title: FTC demands documents from OpenAI and Anthropic, and eight states sue OpenAI
items.what: On October 14 the FTC sent civil investigative demands to OpenAI and Anthropic seeking records on AI safety and security incidents, safeguards, marketing and privacy policies. The same day, eight state attorneys general filed separate lawsuits against OpenAI, alleging ChatGPT was marketed as safe while harming children and vulnerable users.
items.why: There is no federal AI safety law, but consumer protection, privacy and children's laws already apply. If you build or sell AI products, make sure your safety and privacy claims match what the product actually does, and document the safeguards behind them.
expert: FTC: civil investigative demands (reported as 50+ pages each) under its unfair or deceptive practices authority; the FTC confirmed the demands to press but has not published them. Demands to other AI organizations and compelled executive testimony are reported to follow.

States: Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Iowa, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia, each in its own state court. Claims include state consumer protection laws, Montana's Consumer Data Privacy Act, Nebraska's Age-Appropriate Online Design Code Act, and Arkansas children's privacy, product liability and public nuisance claims.
Relief sought includes penalties, disgorgement, injunctions on how ChatGPT operates and limits on collecting minors' data. OpenAI disputes the allegations. Nothing has been adjudicated.
Context: FTC Chair Ferguson co-chairs the White House Super Intelligence Force, which has told AI labs to report and fix rogue model behaviour.
items.cite: FTC civil investigative demands (reported Oct. 15, 2026); state AG complaints filed Oct. 14, 2026.
sources: Troutman Pepper Locke on the state suits

items.title: Critical PHP flaws: cyber agencies urge immediate patching; some Canadian government sites taken offline
items.what: Two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language behind a large share of websites, could let attackers run commands without logging in. Canada's Cyber Centre and the US agency CISA urged organizations to patch at once, and some Government of Canada websites were taken offline as a precaution on October 21.
items.why: If you run websites or web apps, find every system using PHP, starting with internet-facing ones, and patch or isolate them now. If personal information is exposed, breach-reporting duties under privacy law may follow.
expert: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (Cyber Centre alert AL26-026). Fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 according to vendor and security-firm reports; confirm against your software providers' advisories.

Cyber Centre advice (Oct. 21, 2026): identify PHP systems, prioritize internet-facing ones, apply updates, isolate unpatched applications from public networks, and report suspected malicious activity.
Reported as first found with AI agents in August 2026. Montreal's STM and Quebec's SAQ also took sites down as a precaution.
items.cite: Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, AL26-026 and statement (Oct. 21, 2026); CISA alert (Oct. 21, 2026).

items.title: Canada's Privacy Commissioner launches a Children's Privacy Code
items.what: The federal Privacy Commissioner published Canada's first Children's Privacy Code. It expects privacy-protective defaults for children and teens, such as location tracking and third-party sharing off by default, and no profiling of children for targeted advertising. Comments are open until January 20, 2027.
items.why: Canada now has written expectations close to the UK's Children's Code. If young Canadians use your service, compare your defaults and ad practices against it now.
expert: Applies the existing PIPEDA framework (commercial activity only); the release does not say the Code is binding or give an effective date.
Parental consent under 13; opt-in for non-essential uses; no deceptive design; practical correction and deletion; no profiling for marketing or AI-driven decisions.
items.cite: OPC, Children's Privacy Code (Oct. 20, 2026).

items.title: UK will ban under-16s from social media, starting spring 2027
items.what: The UK government announced it will stop under-16s from holding accounts on social media platforms where users post content and algorithms drive feeds. Messaging services are excluded. Ofcom will enforce it.
items.why: If your service lets people post and interact in the UK, check whether it falls in scope and plan for age checks at 16. Ofcom has now named the age-check methods it thinks can work at 16. Other measures were announced too, including a ban on romantic AI chatbots for under-18s.
expert: Regulations to be made under powers added to the Online Safety Act 2023 by the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026.
Timeline as announced: details and exemptions in July 2026, regulations by December 2026, implementation spring 2027.
Also announced: romantic chatbot ban for under-18s, screen-time limits and curfews for 16–18s, restrictions on livestreaming and contact from strangers, and possible action on VPNs.
Ofcom has said age assurance at 16 should be feasible, but fewer methods exist than at 18.

Ofcom rapid assessment (Oct. 29, 2026): four methods can be highly effective at 16 — photo ID matching, banking information, digital identity services and facial age estimation. Credit card, mobile network and email-based checks work at 18 but not at 16; self-declaration and parental consent are not effective. No method is bypass-proof. Ofcom will consult on guidance once draft regulations are published.
items.cite: UK government announcement, June 15, 2026.
sources: Ofcom: rapid assessment of age assurance at 16

items.title: Ofcom is enforcing the Online Safety Act, including against AI features
items.what: Ofcom has fined sites that failed to check users' ages, opened an investigation into X over its Grok chatbot creating sexualised images, and is investigating Telegram. It has also publicly pressed the largest platforms to do more on age checks and grooming.
items.why: The Online Safety Act applies to services with UK users wherever they are based. Generative AI features on a platform are covered, so test what they can produce before launch.
expert: X/Grok investigation opened January 12, 2026, covering illegal-content risk assessment, priority illegal content (intimate image abuse, CSAM), takedown and children's risk assessment. Maximum penalty: £18M or 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue.

Ofcom update (Oct. 14, 2026): X/Grok investigation narrowed to illegal-content and complaints and reporting duties; no provisional decision yet. Ofcom said it could not investigate image generation on the standalone Grok service because of gaps in how the Act covers chatbots; SpaceXAI (formerly xAI) has since restricted images of real people and sexual content for UK users.
Largest fines to date are in the £1M range, against pornography services for failing to use highly effective age assurance.
Ofcom has signalled business disruption applications (payment and advertising withdrawal) against non-compliant sites.
The Crime and Policing Act 2026 extends coverage of AI chatbots.
items.cite: Online Safety Act 2023; Ofcom investigation into X (Jan. 12, 2026).
sources: Ofcom update on X and Grok (Oct. 14, 2026)

items.title: Ofcom investigates Meta over risk checks before launching Instagram's disappearing-photo feature
items.what: Ofcom has opened an investigation into whether Meta carried out proper illegal-content and children's risk assessments before launching Instagram "Instants", a feature for sharing photos and videos that disappear after viewing. Meta says it assessed the risks and briefed Ofcom before launch.
items.why: Under the Online Safety Act, a significant change to a service needs an updated risk assessment before it goes live, not after. If you run a platform with UK users, build the assessment into your launch process for new features.
expert: Opened October 6, 2026. Duties at issue: Online Safety Act 2023, s. 9(4) (illegal content risk assessment) and s. 11(4) (children's risk assessment) in relation to a significant change to the service.
Instants launched May 13, 2026, via Instagram Direct.
Opening an investigation is not a finding of breach. Maximum penalty: £18M or 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue, whichever is greater.
items.cite: Online Safety Act 2023, ss. 9(4), 11(4); Ofcom investigation into Meta Platforms Inc. (Oct. 6, 2026).

items.title: UK competition regulator imposes first digital markets rules on Google search
items.what: Under its new digital markets powers, the CMA has imposed rules on Google search covering fair ranking, data portability and publishers' control over how their content is used, including in AI Overviews. Rules on search choice screens are still being consulted on.
items.why: Publishers and businesses that depend on Google search in the UK now have new rights and a complaints route. Apple and Google have also made commitments on app stores.
expert: Google designated with strategic market status (general search and search advertising) on October 10, 2025; Apple and Google designated for mobile platforms the same month.
Publisher conduct requirement imposed June 3, 2026; fair ranking and data portability on June 17, 2026; further user-choice consultation opened September 23, 2026.
Publisher requirement covers opting out of use in AI Overviews and training of other generative AI models, plus attribution.
Apple and Google mobile commitments (app review fairness, developer data, iOS interoperability) began April 1, 2026; formal conduct requirements remain possible.
items.cite: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, Part 1.

items.title: UK data law changes are phasing in; a complaints procedure was due in June
items.what: The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 amends UK GDPR and the cookie rules. Since June 2026, organisations must have a process for handling data protection complaints. Other changes are being switched on in stages.
items.why: Check that you have a complaints procedure. Some changes make life easier, such as new lawful grounds for certain processing and fewer cookie consent requirements, but fines for marketing and cookie breaches go up to UK GDPR levels.
expert: Royal Assent June 19, 2025. Commencement in stages: smart data and breach-notification changes (Aug. 2025), digital verification services framework (Dec. 2025), complaints-handling duty (June 2026).

Reforms include "recognised legitimate interests", relaxed rules on automated decision-making outside special category data, "reasonable and proportionate" searches for subject access requests, and a "not materially lower" test for international transfers.
The ICO is being replaced by an Information Commission. Check commencement regulations before relying on a provision.
items.cite: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, c. 18.

items.title: UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill cleared the Lords; at Commons November 24
items.what: This bill updates the UK's cyber rules for essential services. It brings managed IT service providers and key suppliers into scope and requires faster reporting of cyber incidents. The Lords passed it at third reading on November 2 with amendments. The Commons considers those amendments on November 24, the last step before Royal Assent.
items.why: If you provide IT services to UK essential services, such as health, energy, water or transport, you may soon be directly regulated. Expect new reporting duties and contract terms from customers.
expert: Amends the Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018.
Extends scope to managed service providers and "designated critical suppliers"; tighter incident reporting (initial notice within 24 hours, full report within 72 hours).
Carried over into the 2026–27 session (King's Speech, May 13, 2026). Lords third reading November 2, 2026; Commons carry-over motion November 4; Commons consideration of Lords amendments November 24.
Government moved to disagree with two Lords amendments: a regime-wide statutory review and a register of foreign powers. If the Lords insist, the bill enters ping-pong.
Outcome of November 24 Commons vote not yet confirmed at publication of this update.
items.cite: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill (DSIT).

items.title: UK shelves plan to let AI firms train on copyrighted work by default
items.what: The government dropped its proposal for a copyright exception allowing AI training unless rights holders opt out. It will gather more evidence and prefers licensing deals between companies.
items.why: Training AI on UK copyrighted material without permission remains legally risky. More consultations are coming, including on deepfakes and labelling AI content.
expert: No text and data mining exception for now; input and output transparency left for further work, with an interim report on output labelling promised for autumn.
Likely removal of copyright for computer-generated works deferred; consultation on deepfake harms and possible personality rights.
Treatment of models trained abroad left open pending litigation such as Getty Images v. Stability AI.
items.cite: UK Government report on copyright and AI, March 23, 2026.

items.title: White House turns to voluntary AI safety: an industry accord and a new 'Super Intelligence' task force
items.what: On September 29, six leading AI developers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI and Nvidia, signed a White House accord committing to internal safety controls, outside audits and board oversight of their most advanced models. The same day, an executive order told federal agencies to call AI "super intelligence". On October 4 the President announced a federal "Super Intelligence Force" to coordinate the government's response to AI risks. The task force held its first meeting on October 15, adopted a charter and told AI companies to report and fix rogue model behaviour. The 60-day deadline for proposed legislative language defining "super intelligence" falls around November 28, 2026.
items.why: There is still no binding federal AI safety law. The accord has no penalties and findings go to company boards, not regulators or the public. If you buy or build on frontier models, ask vendors what they have committed to, but keep planning around state laws, which still apply.
expert: White House Accord on Super Intelligence (Sept. 29, 2026): four layers: (1) internal controls monitoring model capabilities and alignment in areas such as cybersecurity and biosecurity; (2) an empowered internal oversight team; (3) an independent external auditor or evaluator, chosen by the company; (4) an independent board committee receiving reports.

E.O. 14434, Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence (signed Sept. 29, 2026; 91 Fed. Reg. 63129, Oct. 2, 2026): agencies to use "Super Intelligence (SI)" in place of "AI" in official communications; within 60 days (~Nov. 28) the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology proposes legislative language for a federal SI definition (current reference: 15 U.S.C. § 9401(3)).

Super Intelligence Force (announced Oct. 4, 2026): chaired by the Director of National Intelligence, with the FTC Chair among vice chairs; charter mandates plans for responding to SI-enabled threats while preventing overregulation; report due within 120 days (~early February 2027).

First Super Intelligence Force meeting (Oct. 15, 2026): charter adopted; AI labs told to follow a "notification and remediation process" for rogue behaviour; whether it is mandatory, and any penalties, are unclear.
Builds on the June 2, 2026 order "Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security".
Separate from the preemption push under E.O. 14365; the Vice President has rejected FDA- or FAA-style AI regulation.
items.cite: White House Accord on Super Intelligence (Sept. 29, 2026); E.O. 14434, 91 Fed. Reg. 63129 (Oct. 2, 2026); Super Intelligence Force announcement (Oct. 4, 2026).
sources: Nextgov/FCW on the order and accord
TechCrunch on the Super Intelligence Force

items.title: White House pushes to override state AI laws with one national standard
items.what: A December 2025 executive order set up a Justice Department task force to challenge state AI laws. In March 2026 the White House asked Congress for a national AI law that would override most state rules, while letting states keep child-safety and consumer-protection laws.
items.why: For now, state AI laws still apply and must be followed. Congress has twice refused to block state AI laws, so do not plan around preemption until a federal law actually passes. After the Democratic midterms, federal preemption legislation is even less likely in the new Congress.
expert: Executive Order 14365, Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence (Dec. 11, 2025): DOJ AI Litigation Task Force (set up Jan. 9, 2026), review of "onerous" state laws, and BEAD broadband funding conditions.
National AI framework (Mar. 20, 2026) also states that training on copyrighted works is lawful and warns against forcing ideological changes to AI outputs.

The Senate removed a state AI moratorium from the 2025 reconciliation bill (99–1), and preemption was left out of the FY2026 NDAA. Democratic midterm wins make federal preemption legislation unlikely in the 120th Congress.
items.cite: E.O. 14365 (Dec. 11, 2025); White House national AI legislative framework (Mar. 20, 2026).

items.title: Colorado rewrites its AI law; AG rules adopted November 19 — both take effect January 2027
items.what: Colorado replaced the first broad US state AI law with a narrower one aimed at automated decision-making in important areas like jobs, housing, credit and health care. Businesses must tell people when such tools are used, explain bad outcomes, and offer correction and human review. The Attorney General adopted 76 pages of implementing rules on November 19.
items.why: If you use automated tools to make decisions about Colorado residents, prepare notices and an appeal process for January 1, 2027. The Chatbot Safety Act rules are also final.
expert: SB 26-189 repeals and replaces SB 24-205; signed May 2026.

Focus on "automated decision-making technology" in consequential decisions: pre-use disclosure, post-adverse-decision explanation, correction rights, human review on request; three-year record retention.
Attorney General enforcement under the Colorado Consumer Protection Act; no private right of action; 60-day cure period until January 1, 2030.
Rules adopted November 19, 2026 (76 pages). Rules take effect 20 days after Secretary of State publication; exact date not yet confirmed. Treat January 1, 2027 as the operative start date.
ID-only age verification for chatbots banned in the rules; alternative methods required.
First chatbot reports under HB 26-1263 due July 1, 2027.
items.cite: Colorado SB 26-189; HB 26-1263 (Chatbot Safety Act). AG rules adopted Nov. 19, 2026, 4 CCR 904-6.

items.title: California enacts new rules on AI at work, kids' feeds and privacy deletion rights
items.what: California's governor signed a large set of AI and privacy bills by his September 30 deadline. They include limits on using AI alone to discipline or fire workers, a ban on addictive feeds and autoplay for users under 16, wider deletion rights under the state privacy law, and updates to the AI Transparency Act.
items.why: California rules often become the US baseline. If you use automated tools in HR, run a platform used by teens, or handle California consumers' data, review these laws now. Most new California laws take effect January 1, 2027, but check each bill's effective date.
expert: SB 947 (No Robo Bosses Act of 2026): employers may not rely solely on an automated decision system for discipline or termination decisions; human review required.
AB 1883 (workplace surveillance) and SB 951 (notice where an AI system causes a mass layoff, relocation or termination).

AB 1709 (signed Sept. 10): covered platforms may not provide addictive features, such as personalized feeds and autoplay, to users under 16; age verification through the Digital Age Assurance Act; AG enforcement with civil penalties per affected minor.
SB 923 (signed Sept. 27): expands CCPA deletion rights to information collected about a consumer, not only from them; online-only businesses must offer an online request method.

SB 1000 and AB 2713 amend the California AI Transparency Act (provenance data and disclosure tools); SB 1000 removes the 1,000,000 monthly user threshold. AB 2246 replaces the Age-Appropriate Design Code provisions.
Vetoed include AB 1542 (sale of sensitive personal information), SB 903 and AB 2575 (health care AI). Likely targets of federal preemption efforts.

items.title: State AI rules now in force: frontier model transparency and companion chatbots
items.what: California requires developers of the largest AI models to publish safety frameworks and report serious incidents, and has rules for AI companion chatbots. Texas's AI law took effect in January, and many states passed chatbot safety laws in 2026.
items.why: If you offer an AI chatbot to US users, especially one that could be used by minors, check state rules on disclosing that it is AI and on handling self-harm conversations.
expert: California SB 53, Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (signed Sept. 29, 2025; effective Jan. 1, 2026): large frontier developers publish safety frameworks and report critical safety incidents; whistleblower protections.
California SB 243 (companion chatbots): AI disclosure, protocols for suicidal ideation, protections for minors; effective Jan. 1, 2026.
Texas Responsible AI Governance Act effective Jan. 1, 2026. New York RAISE Act on frontier models also enacted.
These are the likely first targets of federal preemption efforts.
items.cite: Cal. SB 53 (2025); Cal. SB 243 (2025); Tex. HB 149 (TRAIGA).
sources: Perkins Coie on California AI bills

items.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act: platforms must remove intimate images within 48 hours
items.what: Since May 19, 2026, platforms must have a way for people to ask for removal of non-consensual intimate images, including AI deepfakes, and must remove them within 48 hours. The FTC is enforcing it and has opened a complaint portal.
items.why: Any platform hosting user content for US users needs a working removal process now. The FTC has named 15 major platforms but the law is not limited to them.
expert: Removal must cover the reported image and known identical copies within 48 hours of a valid request.
FTC complaint portal: TakeItDown.ftc.gov. Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive practices.
Criminal provisions on publishing non-consensual intimate imagery took effect on enactment (May 2025).
items.cite: TAKE IT DOWN Act, Pub. L. 119-12 (2025).

items.title: US KIDS Act passed House — Senate lame-duck prospects fading
items.what: The House passed a children's online safety package by 267 to 117 on June 29. It now goes to the Senate, where the Senate Commerce Committee approved a separate version (KOSA) on August 5. Senate floor time is limited before the 119th Congress ends January 3, 2027. As of late November, prospects are fading for passage this session.
items.why: Not law yet. State children's laws still apply. Watch for the new Democratic-controlled 120th Congress to move this in 2027.
expert: H.R. 7757. House KOSA replaces the Senate's duty of care with a duty to maintain "reasonable policies" on listed harms.
Senate Commerce Committee approved its own KOSA with a duty of care by voice vote on August 5, 2026.
No Senate floor vote set. The two chambers disagree on the duty-of-care provision.
Bloomberg Law (Nov. 2026): prospects are fading for the lame-duck session. Bills die on January 3, 2027 if not passed.
items.cite: Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act, H.R. 7757 (119th Cong.), passed House June 29, 2026.

items.title: Updated COPPA rule now fully in force
items.what: The FTC's updated children's privacy rule took full effect on April 22, 2026. Services aimed at children under 13 need separate parental consent to share data with third parties for advertising, written security programs and data retention limits.
items.why: If any part of your US service is directed at children, check your consent flows, vendor sharing and deletion schedules. The FTC has said children's privacy is an enforcement priority.
expert: Separate verifiable parental consent for disclosures to third parties, including for targeted advertising.
Written information security program; written data retention policy with deletion when no longer needed.
Expanded definition of personal information to include biometric identifiers; additional transparency for safe harbor programs.
items.cite: 16 C.F.R. Part 312, as amended (2025); compliance date April 22, 2026.

items.title: Three more US state privacy laws took effect, bringing the total to about 20
items.what: Indiana, Kentucky and Rhode Island privacy laws took effect on January 1, 2026. Oregon now bans selling data of under-16s, and California tightened its data broker rules.
items.why: There is still no federal privacy law. If you serve US consumers, you need a single program that meets the strictest state rules that apply to you.
expert: Indiana and Kentucky largely follow the Virginia model; Rhode Island has a low threshold (35,000 consumers).
Oregon: no sale of personal data with actual knowledge the consumer is under 16; restrictions on precise geolocation sales.
California: data brokers must disclose sales to foreign actors, governments or AI developers; 45-day deletion processing.
items.cite: Ind. SB 5; Ky. HB 15; R.I. HB 7787/SB 2500.

items.title: US critical infrastructure cyber reporting rule is at final White House review
items.what: CISA has sent its final rule requiring critical infrastructure organizations to report significant cyber incidents within 72 hours and ransom payments within 24 hours to the White House for review, the last step before publication. As of mid-November 2026 it remains listed as pending at the White House OMB.
items.why: If you operate in a US critical infrastructure sector, map out who would report and how, now. Publication is expected before the end of 2026, and the 72-hour window will be hard to meet without a plan.
expert: Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act of 2022 (CIRCIA); NPRM April 2024 with sector- and size-based coverage criteria.

OIRA recorded receipt of the final rule (RIN 1670-AA04) on October 1, 2026, and still listed it as pending as of mid-November 2026. The final text, covered-entity test and effective date are not public until it is published.
CISA updated its cyber incident reporting form in November 2026 as preparation for the broader mandate, but the main rule is not yet published.
Treat the 72-hour and 24-hour clocks as planning assumptions until the final text is out.
items.cite: 6 U.S.C. § 681 et seq. (CIRCIA).
sources: Security.io: final rule enters OMB review (Oct. 5, 2026)

items.title: US declines to renew CUSMA; digital rules are part of the dispute
items.what: At the first joint review on July 1, the US chose not to extend the Canada–US–Mexico trade agreement. It stays in force until 2036 but now goes through yearly reviews. US officials have pointed to Canada's streaming law, news law and cloud procurement as irritants.
items.why: Canadian tech and media rules are now bargaining chips. Expect pressure to soften rules that mainly affect US tech companies.
expert: Under Article 34.7, non-confirmation triggers annual joint reviews; the agreement can be extended at any review.
US Trade Representative flagged the Online Streaming Act, Online News Act, the former digital services tax and Canada's sovereign cloud initiative.
Canada rescinded its digital services tax in June 2025 under US pressure.
items.cite: CUSMA/USMCA Art. 34.7 joint review (July 1, 2026).

items.title: Canada to scrap streamers' Canadian-content payments
items.what: After the CRTC raised streaming services' required contributions to Canadian content to 15% of Canadian revenue in May, Ottawa told it to reconsider. A July court filing showed the government now plans to eliminate the base contribution entirely and fund Canadian content directly instead.
items.why: Foreign streamers' obligations in Canada are being reset, likely to a lighter regime. Nothing is final until the government issues a new direction to the CRTC.
expert: CRTC decision May 21, 2026 raised base contributions from 5% to 15%; Minister directed reconsideration June 3, 2026, citing consumer costs.
Department of Justice letter (July 17, 2026) states intent to eliminate the base contribution and replace it with government funding (about $600M a year).
Implementation through a new policy direction under the Broadcasting Act, which requires publication and a comment period. Online News Act unchanged so far.
items.cite: Online Streaming Act, S.C. 2023, c. 8.

items.title: Canada's Bill C-36 would replace PIPEDA with a tougher privacy law
items.what: The Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act would replace the privacy part of PIPEDA. It was introduced in June; second-reading debate began in the House in early November 2026 but no vote has been scheduled.
items.why: If it passes, penalties could reach $10 million or 3% of worldwide revenue, and people could sue after a regulator finding. Start mapping personal data, especially data sent outside Canada. Bill C-36 cannot come into force until Bill C-34 is also enacted.
expert: New federal commission with direct penalty powers; Federal Court review.
Inferences count as personal information; new "sensitive information" category including children's data and biometrics.
Privacy impact assessment required before transferring personal information outside Canada; right to explanation of significant automated decisions.
AI regulation (former AIDA) not revived.
Coming-into-force provisions contingent on Bill C-34 also being enacted and in force.
Second reading debate: began in the House (Hansard Nov. 3 and ongoing). No vote set as of Nov. 24, 2026.
items.cite: Bill C-36, 45th Parl., 1st Sess. First reading June 15, 2026.

items.title: Canada's Bill C-34 is at committee: hearings underway November 17, 19, 24+
items.what: The Safe Social Media Act would impose safety duties on social media and AI chatbot services, including an under-16 account restriction, AI content labelling and digital safety plans. A new Digital Safety Commission would enforce it. It passed second reading on October 29. The Canadian Heritage committee held its first hearings on November 17 and 19 and has scheduled at least 16 hours of witness testimony.
items.why: Compared with the UK, Canada's under-16 rule is less absolute, since the regulator can exempt services with enough safeguards. Platforms serving both countries should plan for both.
expert: Part 1 enacts the Digital Safety Act; Part 2 creates the Digital Safety Commission of Canada with audit, order and penalty powers.
Covers social media and chatbot services; duties include removing CSAM and non-consensual intimate content, and synthetic content labelling.
Accredited researcher access to platform data through a regulator-supervised process.

CHPC committee hearings: Nov. 17 (meeting 53) and Nov. 19 (meeting 54) held. Witnesses at first hearings included Canadian Constitution Foundation, Raise the Age Canada, Amanda Todd Legacy Society, Kids Help Phone, and OpenMedia. Next session Nov. 24 at 3:30 p.m.; committee approved at least 16 hours of hearings. CHPC accepts written briefs of up to 2,000 words.
items.cite: Bill C-34, 45th Parl., 1st Sess. Introduced June 10, 2026.

items.title: Canada's lawful access bill C-22 — civil society urges Senate amendments before recess
items.what: The bill would make it easier for police and intelligence to get subscriber information from online service providers and would require providers to be able to help with authorized access. It has passed the House and is being studied by the Senate national security committee. On November 24 a letter from 26 rights, refugee and privacy organizations urged the Prime Minister to back targeted amendments before the committee finishes.
items.why: Internet, messaging and hosting providers could face new obligations, including keeping metadata. Senate amendments are still possible and expected before the December recess.
expert: Part 1: Criminal Code changes including expedited subscriber-information confirmation. Part 2: Supporting Authorized Access to Information Act (provider capability obligations).
House amendments: metadata retention reduced from one year to six months; narrow compelled-decryption clause added.
OPC asked for a closed list of subscriber identifiers, a necessity and proportionality test, and clear protection against systemic vulnerabilities in encryption.
Nov. 2, 2026: Privacy Commissioner told SECD subscriber-information demands remain broad for a reasonable-suspicion threshold and "publicly available" is undefined.
Nov. 24, 2026: 26 civil-society organizations wrote to PM Carney urging Senate amendments. Senate votes expected before the December recess.
items.cite: Bill C-22, Lawful Access Act, 2026.
sources: Michael Geist: three fixes for C-22 (Nov. 2026)

items.title: Canada's critical infrastructure cyber law receives Royal Assent
items.what: Operators of designated federally regulated critical systems, in sectors like telecom, banking, energy and transport, must run cybersecurity programs and report cyber incidents. The government also gained powers over telecom security.
items.why: Details depend on regulations still to come. Vendors to these operators should expect new contract terms.
expert: Enacts the Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act and amends the Telecommunications Act; S.C. 2026, c. 9.
Watch for coming-into-force orders and regulations setting reporting windows and designated operators.
items.cite: S.C. 2026, c. 9 (former Bill C-8).

items.title: Canadian privacy regulators find OpenAI broke privacy law in building ChatGPT
items.what: Four Canadian privacy commissioners found OpenAI collected too much personal information to train ChatGPT, without adequate consent, and did not let people correct or delete it. OpenAI agreed to limit personal information used in future training.
items.why: Canada has no AI law, but privacy law is already being applied to AI. Know what personal data is in the AI tools you build or buy.
expert: Joint investigation by the OPC and the Quebec, BC and Alberta commissioners; well-founded and conditionally resolved.
Issues: over-broad training data collection including sensitive information, consent, accuracy, access and deletion, accountability.
items.cite: Joint investigation of OpenAI OpCo, LLC (May 6, 2026).

items.title: Canada's AI approach: a national strategy and a transparency consultation, but no AI law
items.what: Canada launched its "AI for All" strategy in June and consulted until September 23 on labelling AI content, telling people when they deal with AI, and tracking AI incidents. On November 9 it signed a voluntary France-led declaration on sharing early warnings about serious AI and cyber incidents. The ISED transparency consultation results have not yet been published.
items.why: Expect any AI transparency rules to come through targeted measures and international commitments rather than a broad AI act, which is closer to the UK's approach than to Colorado's or California's.
expert: Strategy (June 4, 2026) commits to enshrining a right to privacy, child data protections, a deepfakes bill and a Canada Trusted AI Certification.
ISED consultation (July 23–Sept. 23, 2026) covered AI content detection, AI interaction notices, serious incident tracking and AI agent monitoring. Results not yet published as of Nov. 24.

Nov. 9, 2026 declaration: signed by Canada, France, Bahrain, Finland, Norway and the Netherlands, plus companies including Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, Mistral AI, Hugging Face and Cohere. Commits signatories to align incident classification and share timely information on serious AI control and cyber incidents. Voluntary; the US, China, Google and Meta had not signed as of early reports.
Nov. 19, 2026: Global Privacy Assembly adopted a resolution on privacy-protective agentic AI, sponsored by Canada's Privacy Commissioner.
items.cite: ISED, AI transparency consultation (2026); National AI Strategy (June 4, 2026).
sources: BetaKit: Canada signs AI safety declaration

items.title: US threatens tariffs over the UK's digital services tax
items.what: President Trump threatened tariffs on the UK unless it drops its 2% digital services tax on large tech companies. The UK kept the tax in its 2025 trade deal with the US.
items.why: Canada dropped its digital services tax under similar pressure in 2025. Watch whether the UK holds firm.
expert: UK DST: 2% of revenues from UK users for groups with over £500M global digital revenue and over £25M from UK users.
The US–UK Technology Prosperity Deal (Sept. 2025) covered AI, quantum and nuclear cooperation but did not resolve the DST or set digital trade rules.
items.cite: Finance Act 2020, Part 2 (UK DST).
sources: CSIS on the Tech Prosperity Deal

items.title: UK King's Speech: digital ID, police facial recognition rules and AI sandboxes, but no AI bill
items.what: The government's legislative program includes a voluntary digital ID framework, legal rules for police use of facial recognition, and powers for regulators to run sandboxes for new technology, including AI.
items.why: The UK is regulating AI through existing regulators and sector rules rather than one AI law, a similar path to Canada's.
expert: Digital Access to Services Bill (digital identity; initial use for right-to-work checks).
Police Reform Bill (facial recognition and similar technologies).
Regulating for Growth Bill (cross-sector sandbox powers).
items.cite: King's Speech, May 13, 2026.

items.title: Competition Bureau reports on algorithmic pricing
items.what: Canada's Competition Bureau published what it heard from more than 100 submissions on algorithmic and AI-driven pricing. It says such pricing can help efficiency but raises fairness, transparency and collusion risks.
items.why: There is no new rule yet, but if you use pricing software that draws on competitors' data, review it with competition law in mind. The Privacy Commissioner is now also moving toward guidance on personalized pricing under privacy law (see the ca-surveillancepricing item in the Canadian Privacy Scan).
expert: Consultation ran June 10 – Aug. 4, 2025. No formal guidance issued; the Bureau will keep engaging domestically and internationally.
On November 23, 2026, the Privacy Commissioner appeared before the House ETHI committee on AI use in algorithmic pricing and announced an OPC consultation on the privacy dimensions.
items.cite: Competition Bureau, What We Heard: Algorithmic Pricing and Competition (Jan. 22, 2026).
